Usually an OS on the ROM is only there so it can be installed (factory reset) into the hard drive. Modern operating systems want to be mutable because they need to be updated. So a ROM would only explain it being in the OEM install.

Certainly everyone should have the option of rooting. I bought that hardware, I decide what runs on it. However, the actually privilege escalation mechanism is quite complex, and has some not insignificant concerns.

Any app you grant root to can do whatever they want. There is not a reliable way of tracking precisely what they are doing. Couple this with network-provided instructions to execute, and/or a flawed app that exposes a way to inject code, and you've got a new way into your device.

Another specific example, which I actually have not seen in the wild, but have created as a proof of concept in my own research: Apps from the Play store can be automatically granted Accessibility permissions, and an accessibility service can click on things like a user can. So, you can request root from your own app, and accept the request with that same app, via the accessibility service.

Yes, this can be largely prevented via user education and some simple risk analysis, but a user who doesn't know how to root a phone without a beginner's guide us probably not going to consistently make good decisions regarding this.
